newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless claims suggest labor market pressures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless claims suggest labor market pressures.

text.p: Applications for U.S. jobless benefits last week undershot Wall Street expectations, pointing to further labor market tightness, analysts said.
Jobless claims for the week ended February 1 fell to 325,000 from a revised 337,000 the previous week. Economists in a Reuters poll had forecast 347,000 new claims.
"It suggests there hasn't been any loosening in the labor market, that it does remain tight," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Nearly every week of 1997 has brought a substantial downward revision to the previous week's jobless claims number. Throughout January, the four-week moving average declined.

"It all confirms that some of the high numbers we've seen were distortions around the holidays," said Astrid Adolfson, first vice president and an economist at MCM MoneyWatch Inc. "It probably confirms some weather effects as well."
In the past two months, floods, blizzards and cold weather may have padded the claims figures during some weeks, Adolfson said.

The late-January claims decline evident in Thursday's data will not raise anyone's forecasts for Friday's employment report, economists said. The Labor Department's survey period for January jobs data did not include the weeks ended January 25 or February 1, they said.
But continued low claims figures may change analysts' outlook for this month's employment situation.
"We're re-assessing the employment setting. You could make a case that...the labor force is continuing to remain on the tight side," said Flanagan.
Evidence of that tightness could show up in the February employment report, the most comprehensive reading on the labor market ahead of the Federal Reserve's March 25 policy meeting, analysts said.
Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, said the labor situation may prompt a rate hike next month.
"Most of the ingredients for a tightening are in place, and if the Fed had not shifted last year to a lagging perspective, they would have tightened already," he said.
As usual, the central bank and the financial markets will pay more attention to the more stable monthly employment data than the volatile weekly claims reports, Seto said.
"The variability (in claims data) makes it difficult to determine the conditions in the labor market," he said.
Treasuries dipped modestly after the jobless data, but quickly recovered most of their losses.
